note: Every entry carries two levels. `intermediate` is for a reader meeting the term now; `advanced` is the contested edge, the Malaysian specifics, and how the point is actually argued. The app shows the first on hover and the second behind a toggle, so a lesson can be read without stopping and interrogated when it needs to be. Aliases are what the auto-linker matches in lesson prose; each must be unique across the glossary, and `see` entries are resolved to ids at authoring time.

kinds.latin: A Latin maxim or term of art.
kinds.doctrine: A rule or principle of substantive law.
kinds.statute: A named Act, or a section pinned to one.
kinds.method: How law is studied, researched or argued.

terms.gloss: Protection that no malice defeats.
terms.intermediate: Statements in Parliament and in the course of judicial proceedings, among others. The protection is complete regardless of motive.
terms.advanced: Its scope is narrow precisely because it is absolute: a person defamed on a privileged occasion has no remedy at all, which is a price the law pays for candour in those settings. Statements to the police and in preparation for litigation raise harder questions about how far the protection extends.
terms.source: Standard common law; parliamentary privilege under the Federal Constitution

terms.gloss: Appeal Cases — the English law reports.
terms.intermediate: An English series carrying decisions of the House of Lords, the Privy Council and now the UK Supreme Court. Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593 is one.
terms.advanced: An English citation signals a decision that is at most persuasive here. Use it for structure and vocabulary, which travel; do not assume the substantive position is Malaysian law without checking.

terms.gloss: Assent to a proposal, turning it into a promise.
terms.intermediate: Signifying assent to the proposal. Once communicated in the manner the Act specifies, the proposal becomes a promise and the agreement is formed.
terms.advanced: The moment of completion is what decides the race with a revocation, and s 4(2) splits it: as against the proposer, communication is complete when the acceptance is put into a course of transmission out of the acceptor's power; as against the acceptor, when it comes to the proposer's knowledge. That split is the statutory form of the postal rule and is the step most answers get wrong.

terms.gloss: The person charged in a criminal case.
terms.intermediate: The person the prosecution says committed the offence. Not a defendant — that word belongs to civil cases.
terms.advanced: The accused carries no burden to prove innocence. Where a General Exception is raised, the burden of bringing the case within it falls on the accused on the balance of probabilities, and the prosecution's own burden beyond reasonable doubt is untouched by that.

terms.gloss: A finding that the accused is not guilty.
terms.intermediate: The prosecution did not reach its standard. It does not mean the court found the person innocent, and it is not a finding that nothing happened.
terms.advanced: An acquittal may come at the close of the prosecution case, where no prima facie case is made out, or at the end of the whole trial. Reading it as a finding of innocence is the commonest misunderstanding of a verdict.

terms.gloss: The guilty act — the physical element of an offence.
terms.intermediate: The conduct, together with any circumstances and consequences the offence requires. It must coincide with the mental element.
terms.advanced: As with mens rea, the Code states the physical element offence by offence, so the useful question is which limb of the section the facts satisfy. Omissions are criminal only where a duty to act exists, and causation questions — whether the accused's act caused the prohibited result — belong here rather than to the mental element.

terms.gloss: Whether evidence may be received at all.
terms.intermediate: A question logically prior to weight. Under the Evidence Act it is answered by finding the section that declares the fact relevant.
terms.advanced: Admissibility and weight are routinely conflated in answers. Evidence that gets in may still be worth very little, and a court that admits it is not obliged to act on it; conversely, compelling material that no section admits simply cannot be used. Illegally obtained evidence is generally admissible in Malaysia if relevant, which surprises students trained on other systems.

terms.gloss: Illustration (g) to s 114 — withheld evidence would have been unfavourable.
terms.intermediate: The court may presume that evidence which could be and is not produced would, if produced, be unfavourable to the person withholding it.
terms.advanced: It is permissive, not automatic, and it is not drawn from every gap in the evidence. The party inviting it must show that the evidence was available and material and that no explanation for its absence has been given; failing to call a witness whose evidence would merely repeat what is already proved does not attract it.

terms.gloss: Written evidence, sworn or affirmed to be true.
terms.intermediate: A statement of facts put in writing and sworn. Most applications before trial are decided on affidavits rather than on witnesses giving evidence aloud.
terms.advanced: Because the maker is not cross-examined, an affidavit is weak where the facts are genuinely disputed — which is why a real dispute of fact points towards a writ and a trial rather than an originating summons.

terms.gloss: Electing to keep a contract alive despite a right to end it.
terms.intermediate: Signifying by words or conduct that the contract continues, which extinguishes the right to terminate for that breach.
terms.advanced: Affirmation is easier to commit than students expect: continuing to demand performance, accepting further benefits, or simply delaying can all amount to it. It matters equally in rescission for misrepresentation, where affirming after discovering the truth bars avoidance.

terms.gloss: Attorney General's Chambers.
terms.intermediate: The government body that publishes the official text of Malaysian Acts, free, on its portal. That is the source to use for statute.
terms.advanced: A page printed from the portal is not a copy of the Gazette, which matters only where something formal turns on the exact printed text. For study and ordinary research it is exactly what you want.

terms.gloss: Annual general meeting.
terms.intermediate: The yearly meeting of a company's members. It is where accounts are laid, directors appointed and resolutions voted on.
terms.advanced: Notice, quorum and the majority required are conditions of a valid resolution rather than formalities. A private company under the 2016 Act is not required to hold one, which older textbooks do not reflect.

terms.gloss: A promise or set of promises the parties have made to each other.
terms.intermediate: What the two sides have agreed. Not every agreement is a contract: it becomes one only when the Act's requirements are met.
terms.advanced: Section 2 builds it in steps — proposal, acceptance, promise, agreement — and s 10 then adds what turns an agreement into a contract: free consent, capacity, lawful consideration and a lawful object. Naming the step you are on keeps the analysis straight.

terms.gloss: All India Reporter.
terms.intermediate: The main Indian law report series. Indian authority matters here more than in most jurisdictions, because the Penal Code and the Evidence Act share Indian ancestry.
terms.advanced: Where a Malaysian provision descends from the Indian original, Indian decisions on the same wording are genuinely useful. That is a reason to read them with care, not a licence to treat them as binding.

terms.gloss: All Malaysia Reports.
terms.intermediate: A third Malaysian law report series. Seeing a case cited to AMR rather than MLJ or CLJ does not make it any less authoritative.
terms.advanced: Which series a judgment appears in is a publishing fact, not a legal one. What decides weight is the court that decided it, which is why a citation without the court in brackets cannot be weighed.

terms.gloss: Asking a higher court to reconsider a decision.
terms.intermediate: A challenge to a decision, heard by a court above the one that made it. The question is whether the decision was right — which is not the question judicial review asks.
terms.advanced: An appeal is a creature of statute: there is no inherent right to one, so the first question is always which provision gives it and whether leave is required. An appeal against a finding of fact faces a heavy burden, because the trial court saw the witnesses and the appellate court does not.

terms.gloss: The party who brings an appeal.
terms.intermediate: Whoever is asking the higher court to change the decision. That may be either side, depending on who lost.
terms.advanced: The label follows the appeal rather than the original action, so a plaintiff who won at trial becomes the respondent on the defendant's appeal. Getting this backwards makes a procedural history unreadable.

terms.gloss: Putting the rule against these facts, rather than restating it.
terms.intermediate: The part of an answer that does the reasoning: taking the rule you have stated and working out what it means for the facts in front of you, both ways where the point is arguable.
terms.advanced: This is where most marks sit and where most are lost. The test of a real application paragraph is whether it could be moved to another problem without alteration — if it could, it is still rule statement. Arguing both ways and then deciding is what separates it from assertion.
terms.source: Rubric band used throughout this app

terms.gloss: Dividing responsibility between claimant and defendant.
terms.intermediate: The exercise s 12 of the Civil Law Act 1956 requires: reducing damages to the extent just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in the responsibility for the damage.
terms.advanced: Share in the responsibility takes account of both blameworthiness and the causative potency of each party's conduct, so a small piece of carelessness that made a large difference can attract a substantial reduction. Appellate courts are reluctant to interfere with a trial judge's apportionment, which is why the reasoning behind the figure matters more than the figure.

terms.gloss: Taking a person into custody, with constitutional safeguards attached.
terms.intermediate: Article 5(3) requires that the person be told the grounds as soon as may be and allowed to consult a legal practitioner of his choice; Art 5(4) sets the twenty-four hour limit.
terms.advanced: Whether the arrest was lawful matters beyond the arrest itself: it affects the admissibility of what followed, the lawfulness of any resistance, and any claim for false imprisonment. The right to counsel under Art 5(3) is not always given effect at the moment of arrest, and the case law on when access must be allowed is worth reading rather than summarising.
terms.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(3) and 5(4); Criminal Procedure Code

terms.gloss: Freedom of speech, assembly and association — and the restrictions on them.
terms.intermediate: Article 10(1) confers the rights on citizens; Article 10(2) allows Parliament to impose such restrictions as it deems necessary or expedient on a closed list of grounds.
terms.advanced: Whether a restriction falls within a permitted head is for the court, not for Parliament's own characterisation of it; how hard the court may look beyond that is the unresolved argument in the area, with Pung Chen Choon and Sivarasa Rasiah pulling in different directions and neither overruling the other. The effect of a law matters more than its form: a statute that never mentions speech can restrict it, and the court looks at what it does.
terms.source: Federal Constitution Art 10; PP v Pung Chen Choon [1994] 1 MLJ 566 (FC); Sivarasa Rasiah v Badan Peguam Malaysia [2010] 2 MLJ 333 (FC)

terms.gloss: Civil courts have no jurisdiction over matters within Syariah jurisdiction.
terms.intermediate: Inserted in 1988. It subtracts jurisdiction from the civil courts where a matter already lies within the Syariah courts' jurisdiction — it does not grant the Syariah courts anything.
terms.advanced: Because it is a subtraction, the clause does nothing unless the matter is within Syariah jurisdiction in the first place, and that jurisdiction comes from State enactments under List II and reaches only persons professing the religion of Islam. Indira Gandhi held that the clause does not oust the civil courts' inherent power of judicial review. The common misstatement — 'if Islam is involved the civil court has no jurisdiction' — is neither what it says nor what it does.
terms.source: Federal Constitution Art 121(1A); Indira Gandhi a/p Mutho v Pengarah Jabatan Agama Islam Perak [2018] 1 MLJ 545 (FC)

terms.gloss: The Federal Court's exclusive constitutional jurisdiction.
terms.intermediate: The Federal Court alone determines whether a law is invalid for want of legislative competence, and disputes between States or between the Federation and a State.
terms.advanced: A constitutional question arising in the High Court may be referred upward rather than decided there, and the mechanism and its limits sit in the Constitution and the Courts of Judicature Act 1964. Reaching the right constitutional conclusion in the wrong forum has not advised the client, which is why forum is a method point rather than a formality.
terms.source: Federal Constitution Art 128; Courts of Judicature Act 1964

terms.gloss: The supremacy clause.
terms.intermediate: 'This Constitution is the supreme law of the Federation and any law passed after Merdeka Day which is inconsistent with this Constitution shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.'
terms.advanced: Clauses (3) and (4) then restrict how a challenge on the ground of legislative competence may be brought, including a leave requirement for proceedings in the Federal Court. That is a procedural trap rather than a substantive one, and it is where otherwise competent answers lose marks — check the current text and practice before saying how such a challenge is commenced.

terms.gloss: Liberty of the person, and the safeguards on arrest.
terms.intermediate: No person may be deprived of life or personal liberty save in accordance with law; an arrested person must be told the grounds, allowed counsel, and produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours.
terms.advanced: Article 5 speaks of persons, not citizens, so it protects anyone within the jurisdiction. 'In accordance with law' has carried a good deal of weight in the case law: read thinly it means any validly enacted procedure, read thickly it imports a requirement that the law itself be fair, and which reading applies is one of the live questions in Malaysian constitutional law.

terms.gloss: Federal law prevails over inconsistent State law.
terms.intermediate: Where a State law is inconsistent with a federal law, the federal law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
terms.advanced: Article 75 presupposes a valid federal law: if the federal statute is itself outside List I and List III it prevails over nothing and is void under Art 4(1). Answers that reach for Art 75 first have skipped the question that usually decides the case.

terms.gloss: Parliament legislating on State matters for uniformity.
terms.intermediate: The provision that lets Parliament make law on a State subject for the purpose of promoting uniformity, with the law taking effect in a State only when adopted by its legislature.
terms.advanced: This is the answer to the obvious objection that land is a State matter and the National Land Code is federal. It is also the reason the Code's application is not uniform across the whole Federation — Sabah and Sarawak have their own land legislation, and the position there is not a footnote to the Code but a different statutory scheme.

terms.gloss: Equality before the law and equal protection.
terms.intermediate: All persons are equal before the law and entitled to its equal protection, with express exceptions the Constitution itself provides for.
terms.advanced: Equality does not require identical treatment: the working doctrine is reasonable classification, asking whether the distinction rests on an intelligible differentia and whether that differentia bears a rational relation to the object of the law. Sivarasa Rasiah is the route by which proportionality has been argued into Malaysian constitutional analysis through Art 8(1).

terms.gloss: Hear the other side.
terms.intermediate: A person liable to be affected by a decision must be given notice of the case against him and a fair opportunity to answer it.
terms.advanced: The content is variable but the core is not: notice of the substance of the allegations, and a real chance to respond. Telling someone only that 'complaints have been considered' fails it on any view, because there is nothing to answer. Whether an oral hearing or legal representation is required is the arguable part.

terms.gloss: An offence for which bail is available as of right.
terms.intermediate: A person accused of a bailable offence shall be released on bail under s 387. It is not a discretion.
terms.advanced: The confusing label is the next one: 'non-bailable' does not mean bail is unavailable, only that it lies in the court's discretion under s 388. A third category, where the offence is punishable with death or imprisonment for life, attracts the restrictions in s 388(1) subject to its provisos for young persons, women and the sick or infirm.
terms.source: Criminal Procedure Code ss 387 and 388, First Schedule

terms.gloss: British and Irish Legal Information Institute.
terms.intermediate: A free website carrying the full text of British and Irish judgments. Useful for reading an English case you have seen cited.
terms.advanced: Free databases give you the text and not the later history. Nothing on a free portal tells you a case was later reversed, and silence there is not evidence that it was not.

terms.gloss: The civil standard: more likely than not.
terms.intermediate: What a plaintiff must establish to succeed, and the standard to which an accused discharges any burden a statute places on him.
terms.advanced: Because it is lower than the criminal standard, the same facts can lose a prosecution and win a suit — that is the system working as designed, not an inconsistency. Fraud alleged in civil proceedings is proved to this standard in Malaysia rather than the criminal one, though that is a point whose current statement should be checked.

terms.gloss: The argument that some constitutional features survive even a valid amendment.
terms.intermediate: That certain features — judicial power, the rule of law, the separation of powers — are so fundamental that Parliament cannot remove them by amending the Constitution.
terms.advanced: Its origin is Indian and its reception in Malaysia has changed direction more than once, with Federal Court decisions both rejecting and applying it. It is an argument of last resort against an amendment, not a general licence to strike down legislation, and conflating the two is the commonest error in an answer. If you write about it, write about the sequence of authority and give the citations.
terms.source: Malaysian and Indian constitutional case law

terms.gloss: The criminal standard of proof.
terms.intermediate: The prosecution must prove its case to that standard on the whole of the evidence. A defence that raises a reasonable doubt succeeds; it does not have to be believed.
terms.advanced: The burden does not shift, except where a statute places one on the accused — s 105 of the Evidence Act for the general exceptions being the main example, and that is discharged on the balance of probabilities. Writing that the accused must 'prove' his defence at the close of the case is wrong outside those statutory instances.
terms.source: Evidence Act 1950 s 105; Criminal Procedure Code s 182A

terms.gloss: A decision a court has no choice but to follow.
terms.intermediate: A decision of a superior court in the same hierarchy, on the same point of law. A court faced with one must either follow it or distinguish it.
terms.advanced: Only the ratio binds; the rest of the judgment is persuasive. Decisions of courts of coordinate jurisdiction — one High Court on another — are not binding, though in practice they are followed unless there is good reason not to, because inconsistency at the same level is itself a mischief.

terms.gloss: Failing to perform what the contract required.
terms.intermediate: Non-performance, defective performance, or a refusal to perform. It gives the innocent party a right to damages, and sometimes a right to terminate.
terms.advanced: Not every breach permits termination. Section 40 gives the right to put an end to the contract where a party has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety — and that right is an election which is lost by acquiescence in the contract's continuance. A party who keeps pressing for performance after a repudiation may be held to have affirmed and left himself with damages only.

terms.gloss: Falling below the standard the law required.
terms.intermediate: The second element of negligence, measured against the reasonable person in the defendant's position — with the standard raised where the defendant holds himself out as having a skill.
terms.advanced: The standard is objective, so inexperience is no answer, and it is fixed by what was reasonable at the time rather than with hindsight. A defendant's departure from its own written procedure is strong evidence of breach without being conclusive: the standard is the reasonable person's, and a method statement can set the bar higher than the law does.

terms.gloss: A safe harbour for honest, informed commercial decisions.
terms.intermediate: Section 214: a director who makes a business judgement in good faith for a proper purpose, without a material personal interest, on a reasonably informed basis and in the reasonable belief that it is in the company's best interest, is taken to have met the duty of care.
terms.advanced: Its point is that courts should not second-guess commercial risk with hindsight. Each condition has to be satisfied, and the two that most often fail are the absence of a material personal interest and the requirement of a reasonably informed basis — a decision taken without inquiry does not qualify however honestly it was made.

terms.gloss: Would the damage have happened anyway?
terms.intermediate: The test of factual causation: but for the defendant's breach, would the claimant have suffered the loss? If it would have happened anyway, causation fails.
terms.advanced: The classic illustration is a casualty officer who negligently sends away a man already fatally poisoned: the breach is plain and the claim fails, because correct treatment would have made no difference. Establishing the counterfactual is an evidential question, and in clinical cases it usually requires expert evidence about what proper treatment would have achieved.

terms.gloss: The gap between the mark you predicted and the mark you gave yourself.
terms.intermediate: A measure of whether your sense of your own work matches what a rubric says about it. This app records the prediction before the rubric is shown, and cannot let you revise it.
terms.advanced: A consistent over-estimate is the failure mode that survives a whole degree, because it is invisible from the inside: you cannot correct a gap you do not believe is there. Under-estimating costs less but makes a good answer hard to tell from a lucky one. The figure only compares one judgment against another you made minutes later, so it catches drift, not a learner who is generously wrong about both.
terms.source: The problem-question layer of this app

terms.gloss: Whether the breach actually caused the damage — in fact and in law.
terms.intermediate: Factual causation uses the but-for test; legal causation asks whether a later event broke the chain.
terms.advanced: The but-for test breaks down in two recognised situations: multiple sufficient causes, and scientific uncertainty about which of several exposures caused the injury. Both have generated exceptional approaches, and both should be identified as exceptions rather than used as the general rule. A breach that caused no loss defeats the claim however plain the carelessness.

terms.gloss: The set of facts giving a right to sue.
terms.intermediate: Every element that must be proved for the claim to succeed. It is what a pleading must disclose and what limitation runs from.
terms.advanced: The date of accrual is the date the last necessary element falls into place — which in negligence means damage, not carelessness. That is why a claim can be time-barred before the claimant knew there was anything to complain about, and why latent damage is such a persistent problem.
terms.source: Limitation Act 1953; Rules of Court 2012 O 18 r 19

terms.gloss: The narrow ground on which a chargor resists an order for sale.
terms.intermediate: What the chargor must show to prevent sale: not a general discretion, but a defect going to the chargee's right to the order.
terms.advanced: The recognised categories are narrow — that the chargee has failed to meet a condition precedent, that the charge is unlawful or unenforceable, or that the order would be contrary to some rule of law or equity. Financial hardship is not cause to the contrary, however sympathetic, and advising otherwise raises expectations the statute will not meet.
terms.source: National Land Code; the Malaysian case law on cause to the contrary

terms.gloss: An entry freezing dealings while a claim is worked out.
terms.intermediate: A private caveat may be entered by a person claiming title, a registrable interest, or a beneficial entitlement under a trust affecting the land. It prevents registration of dealings while in force.
terms.advanced: A caveat creates no interest — it is a freeze, not a right — and it lapses after the statutory period unless extended. On an application to remove it the caveator must show a serious question to be tried and that the balance of convenience favours maintaining it, which is the interlocutory injunction shape for the same reason. Entering one without reasonable cause exposes the caveator to compensation, so it is not a costless holding move.
terms.source: National Land Code s 323 and the caveat provisions

terms.gloss: An order quashing a decision.
terms.intermediate: The principal remedy in judicial review: the decision is set aside, and the matter is generally remitted for reconsideration according to law.
terms.advanced: It goes with the other prerogative orders — prohibition to restrain a decision not yet made, and mandamus to compel the performance of a public duty. In Malaysia they are sought under Order 53 together with declarations and injunctions, and damages may be claimed in the same proceedings in the circumstances the rule allows.

terms.gloss: The Code's security interest over registered land.
terms.intermediate: Created by a registered instrument. It gives the chargee no possession — the security is the ability to enforce, not to occupy.
terms.advanced: On default the chargee serves the statutory notice and, if it is not remedied, applies for an order for sale. The route depends on the title: Registry title goes to the High Court, Land Office title to the Land Administrator. Identifying which before saying where the application goes is where the method marks in a charge question sit.
terms.source: National Land Code, the charge provisions

terms.gloss: Inducing delivery of property by deception.
terms.intermediate: Section 415. The accused deceived a person and thereby fraudulently or dishonestly induced that person to deliver property, or to do or omit something he would not otherwise have done.
terms.advanced: Consent is present but vitiated by the deception, which places it on the third branch of the possession question. The deception must have induced the delivery, so a lie that made no difference to the victim's decision is not cheating however dishonest — causation matters here as much as it does in tort.

terms.gloss: A tool that tells you whether a case is still good law.
terms.intermediate: A service tracking a judgment's subsequent judicial treatment — whether it has been followed, distinguished, doubted or overruled.
terms.advanced: There is no free Malaysian citator, which is the hard limit on free research in this jurisdiction: the AGC portal and CommonLII give you the text and say nothing about status. A portal showing no overruling is not evidence that there was none; it is evidence that the portal does not track it. That check needs a paid service or a systematic search for later cases citing the decision.

terms.gloss: The statute receiving English common law, with cut-off dates.
terms.intermediate: Section 3(1) directs the courts to apply the common law of England and the rules of equity as administered there on stated dates — 7 April 1956 for West Malaysia, with different dates for Sabah and Sarawak.
terms.advanced: The reception is subject to two qualifications that do real work: it applies only so far as local circumstances permit, and only where no local statute makes provision. Section 6 excludes English land law altogether, which is what protects the Torrens system from being undercut by imported doctrines of notice. In practice Malaysian courts cite post-1956 English decisions constantly, and how that squares with the section is a respectable argument rather than a settled one.

terms.gloss: Current Law Journal.
terms.intermediate: A Malaysian law report series, alongside the MLJ. The same case is often reported in both, with different volume and page numbers.
terms.advanced: CLJ also runs one of the subscription citators, which is the tool that tells you what later courts did with a case. That check cannot be done from free sources alone.

terms.gloss: Commonwealth Law Reports — the Australian series.
terms.intermediate: The main Australian law reports. Rogers v Whitaker (1992) 175 CLR 479 is cited in the negligence material.
terms.advanced: Australian authority carries no more weight here than English, and sometimes less familiarity. It is worth citing where a Malaysian court has actually adopted the reasoning, which is the case with Rogers v Whitaker on advice and disclosure.

terms.gloss: A subject governed by a statute that states the rules, not by case law.
terms.intermediate: Contract, criminal law and evidence in Malaysia are codified: the Contracts Act 1950, the Penal Code and the Evidence Act 1950 state the rules, and reasoning begins with their words.
terms.advanced: The consequence is a discipline about authority. An English case is useful where the Act raises the same question and worthless where it does not, and a proposition drawn from English law that contradicts the section is simply wrong — the frequent example is treating past consideration as no consideration when s 2(d) says otherwise. Codes are also read as a whole, so a definition section governs the whole Act.
terms.source: Contracts Act 1950; Penal Code; Evidence Act 1950

terms.gloss: Committing a Penal Code offence, or unlawfully detaining property, to force an agreement.
terms.intermediate: Section 15's definition, which is considerably narrower than the ordinary idea of pressure or the English concept of duress.
terms.advanced: Because the definition is tied to the Penal Code, commercial pressure that would be argued as economic duress in England has no obvious home in s 15, and how far Malaysian law recognises economic duress is a question to check rather than assume. Where coercion is made out the agreement is voidable at the option of the party coerced, and s 73 provides for repayment of money paid under coercion.

terms.gloss: The moment the Act fixes for a proposal, an acceptance or a revocation taking effect.
terms.intermediate: Section 4 gives each kind of communication its own moment, and different moments as against each party. Getting the right one is the whole of a formation-race problem.
terms.advanced: The trap sits in s 4(3)(b): a revocation is complete as against the person to whom it is made when it comes to his knowledge — not when it is delivered. A letter sitting unopened on a desk has been delivered and not communicated, and a problem that mentions an unopened envelope is testing exactly that.

terms.gloss: The statute governing companies in Malaysia.
terms.intermediate: Act 777, which repealed the Companies Act 1965 and changed a great deal: a single optional constitution, no authorised capital, no par value, and single-member private companies.
terms.advanced: This is the module where an out-of-date text does the most damage. A source that refers to the memorandum and articles, or to authorised capital, as current law is describing a repealed statute. Directors' duties are now stated in ss 213 and 218, with a business judgement rule in s 214, and the members' remedies in ss 346 to 350.

terms.gloss: A body corporate with a legal personality of its own.
terms.intermediate: A separate legal person, distinct from the people who own and run it. It can own property, sign contracts, sue and be sued in its own name — and it owes its own debts.
terms.advanced: Separate personality is the idea the rest of company law follows from. Limited liability is a consequence of it rather than the idea itself: because the company owes the debt, a member risks only what remains unpaid on their shares.

terms.gloss: The price of a promise — and in Malaysia, a statutory definition.
terms.intermediate: Under s 2(d), an act or abstinence or promise done at the desire of the promisor, by the promisee or any other person. Section 26 makes an agreement without it void, subject to three exceptions.
terms.advanced: Two departures from English law are decisive. 'Has done or abstained from doing' means past consideration is good consideration here. 'The promisee or any other person' means consideration need not move from the promisee — though that does not abolish privity, and a stranger to the contract still cannot sue on it. Explanation 2 to s 26 adds that inadequacy does not void the agreement but may bear on whether consent was free.

terms.gloss: How a court reads a piece of writing to settle what it means.
terms.intermediate: Working out what words mean in law — in a statute, a contract or a document. Nothing to do with building.
terms.advanced: Construction is a question of law, which is why it can be decided on affidavit without a trial. Where a provision is capable of two readings, the one that promotes the Act's purpose is preferred under s 17A of the Interpretation Acts.

terms.gloss: An agreement the law will enforce.
terms.intermediate: An agreement that meets what the Act requires, so a court will hold the parties to it. Free consent, capacity, a lawful price and a lawful purpose are the four requirements.
terms.advanced: Section 10 is the gate, and each of its limbs opens onto its own body of law: consent onto the vitiating factors, capacity onto s 11, and lawful object onto s 24. An answer that asserts a contract exists without naming which limb is in issue has skipped the analysis.

terms.gloss: The Constitution outranks every other law; inconsistent law is void.
terms.intermediate: Article 4(1) provides that law passed after Merdeka Day which is inconsistent with the Constitution is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
terms.advanced: Two details are routinely dropped. First, the invalidity is partial — 'to the extent of the inconsistency' — so severance is the ordinary course rather than striking down a whole Act. Second, describing Parliament as sovereign is not a loose way of saying it is powerful; it is a category error carried over from English texts and it undermines every constitutional argument built on top of it.

terms.gloss: The statute governing contract in Malaysia.
terms.intermediate: A code covering formation, consideration, free consent, performance, breach and remedies. It is the starting point for every contract question, ahead of any English case.
terms.advanced: Its structure follows the Indian Contract Act 1872, which is why Indian authority is often closer on the wording than English authority is. Several sections depart from English law in ways that decide cases — past consideration is good under s 2(d), consideration may move from a third party, and s 26 saves three promises that would otherwise fail for want of consideration.

terms.gloss: The claimant's own carelessness, reducing the award.
terms.intermediate: Section 12 of the Civil Law Act 1956: where damage results partly from the claimant's own fault, the claim is not defeated but damages are reduced as the court thinks just and equitable.
terms.advanced: Before the section it was a complete defence, which is why older material must be read with care. It is now an apportionment exercise, and an answer should reason to a proportion by reference to the claimant's share in the responsibility rather than asserting that damages 'will be reduced'. It is distinct from novus actus, which defeats the claim outright.

terms.gloss: A court's finding that the accused is guilty.
terms.intermediate: The formal decision that the prosecution proved its case. Punishment follows conviction; the two are separate steps.
terms.advanced: A conviction requires proof beyond reasonable doubt on the whole of the evidence. It is not a finding that the accused probably did it, which is why the same facts can fail a prosecution and still succeed in a civil suit.

terms.gloss: The separation between a company and its members — and when courts look behind it.
terms.intermediate: Lifting the veil means treating the company and its controllers as one. It is done rarely and on stated grounds.
terms.advanced: The recognised routes are statutory — an Act expressly imposing liability, such as s 540 on fraudulent trading — and, at common law, the use of the corporate form to evade an existing obligation or conceal wrongdoing. Genuine agency is a third route but requires an actual agency relationship, not merely control. 'Lifting the veil in the interests of justice' is not a ground however often it is asserted.
terms.source: Companies Act 2016 s 540; the Malaysian case law on lifting the veil

terms.gloss: Hears appeals from the High Court, usually in threes.
terms.intermediate: The intermediate appellate court. For most litigants it is in practice the last court that will hear the case on the merits.
terms.advanced: It binds the High Court and the subordinate courts and is bound by the Federal Court. A Court of Appeal decision that conflicts with an earlier one of its own creates a genuine difficulty for a first-instance judge, and the usual resolution is to follow the later, fuller reasoning while noting the conflict.

terms.gloss: A person to whom money is owed.
terms.intermediate: Whoever is owed the money. A supplier waiting to be paid and a bank waiting for a loan repayment are both creditors.
terms.advanced: Creditors deal with the company, not its members, which is what separate personality means in practice: they take everything the company owns first, and only a guarantee or a statute reaches the people behind it.

terms.gloss: Misappropriating property you were lawfully entrusted with.
terms.intermediate: Section 405. The accused was entrusted with property, or with dominion over it, and dishonestly misappropriated or converted it, or used or disposed of it in violation of a legal direction.
terms.advanced: Entrustment is what separates it from theft: the property came to the accused lawfully. Whether an employee has entrustment or mere custody depends on the scope of what was committed to him, and that question decides which charge fits. The same facts can support alternative charges, and saying which is the better one is part of the answer.

terms.gloss: The statute governing arrest, bail, charge and criminal trial.
terms.intermediate: Act 593. Its First Schedule classifies every offence as seizable or non-seizable and as bailable, non-bailable or unbailable, and that classification decides most of the procedure.
terms.advanced: Look the offence up before reasoning about it — the classification, not the seriousness, is what determines whether police may arrest without warrant and whether bail is a right or a discretion. Special legislation, particularly on security and drugs, frequently displaces the Code's scheme with its own, so the statute creating the offence must be checked too.

terms.gloss: Causing death with the intention or knowledge s 299 specifies.
terms.intermediate: The genus of which murder is the species: causing death by an act done with intention to cause death, or intention to cause bodily injury likely to cause death, or knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.
terms.advanced: Every murder is culpable homicide; not every culpable homicide is murder. The route through a homicide problem is to establish culpable homicide under s 299, then ask whether any limb of s 300 elevates it to murder, then whether any Exception to s 300 brings it back down. Skipping to s 300 because someone died inverts the structure.
aliases: culpable homicide not amounting to murder

terms.gloss: Money awarded as compensation.
terms.intermediate: A sum the court orders one side to pay the other to make up for a loss. Damages compensate; they are not usually a punishment.
terms.advanced: The measure differs by cause of action: in contract the aim is to put the plaintiff where performance would have, in tort where the wrong had not occurred. Note the spelling trap — damage is the harm, damages is the money.
terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 s 74; standard common law

terms.gloss: A transaction in registered land that takes effect on registration.
terms.intermediate: Transfers, leases, charges and easements under the Code. Until the instrument is registered it passes nothing at law.
terms.advanced: This is the point at which a sale and purchase agreement is misdescribed as making the buyer the owner. It does not: it creates contractual rights and an interest capable of protection, and the register decides ownership. Getting that wrong unravels an entire answer on competing interests and priorities.

terms.gloss: A person who owes money.
terms.intermediate: Whoever owes the money. Winning a case makes you a judgment creditor and the other side a judgment debtor — which is not the same as being paid.
terms.advanced: A judgment against a debtor with nothing is worth nothing, so what a defendant can actually pay is a question to ask before suing rather than after. Enforcement is a separate exercise with its own procedures and costs.

terms.gloss: Publishing words that lower a person's reputation.
terms.intermediate: Three elements: the words are defamatory, they refer to the plaintiff, and they were published to at least one person other than the plaintiff.
terms.advanced: All three must be established before any defence arises, and an answer that opens with qualified privilege has assumed the case it should be proving. The libel–slander distinction still matters because slander generally requires proof of special damage, subject to the statutory exceptions in the Defamation Act 1957. Malice is not an element: it defeats two of the defences.

terms.gloss: The person a civil claim is brought against.
terms.intermediate: The side being sued. They answer the claim in a defence, and an allegation the defence does not answer is generally taken as admitted.
terms.advanced: Keep the defendant in a civil suit apart from the accused in a criminal trial; the words are not interchangeable, and using them loosely signals working from an English text. A defendant who files nothing risks judgment in default, with the merits never examined.

terms.gloss: The immediate transferee under a bad instrument takes a defeasible title.
terms.intermediate: Indefeasibility is postponed one step: the person registered on a forged or void instrument can be unwound, but a later bona fide purchaser for value cannot.
terms.advanced: The competing rule, immediate indefeasibility, protects even the immediate transferee and was what Adorna Properties adopted. Tan Ying Hong restored the deferred position, treating the proviso to s 340(3) as protecting subsequent purchasers rather than the immediate one. Which rule applies decides who bears the loss when a title is forged, so it is never a merely academic distinction.
terms.source: National Land Code s 340(3); Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC)

terms.gloss: The probability of recall you are scheduling for.
terms.intermediate: The target the scheduler aims at when it sets the next interval — 0.90 by default, meaning you expect to recall about nine cards in ten when they come up.
terms.advanced: It is a cost dial, not a quality dial: higher retention means many more reviews for a small gain, lower means fewer reviews and more lapses. It should be left alone until several thousand reviews are logged, because the estimate it feeds is noisy before then.

terms.gloss: A person appointed to manage a company.
terms.intermediate: Someone who runs the company and signs for it. Directors owe their duties to the company itself, not to the shareholders individually.
terms.advanced: The statutory duties sit alongside the older equitable ones rather than replacing them. The care-and-skill standard has a floor every director must meet and rises for one who happens to know more, so an accountant on the board is held higher than a lay member.

terms.gloss: Statutory fiduciary and care obligations owed to the company.
terms.intermediate: Section 213(1) requires a director to act for a proper purpose and in good faith in the best interest of the company; s 213(2) requires reasonable care, skill and diligence. Section 218 deals with improper use of position, property or information.
terms.advanced: The care duty has an objective floor and a subjective addition: what may reasonably be expected of a director with those responsibilities, plus any extra knowledge or experience the director actually has. Section 214's business judgement rule is a safe harbour for s 213(2) only — it does not excuse a breach of the fiduciary duty in s 213(1).

terms.term: discharge not amounting to an acquittal
terms.gloss: A discharge that leaves the accused liable to be recharged.
terms.intermediate: The prosecution is stopped but not concluded: the same facts may be charged again. An acquittal, by contrast, is final.
terms.advanced: The distinction has to be explained to a client in terms, because 'discharged' is heard as 'finished'. It also matters to any argument about autrefois acquit: only an acquittal supports the plea, and a discharge leaves the accused exposed indefinitely subject to the Public Prosecutor's discretion.
terms.source: Criminal Procedure Code; Federal Constitution Art 145(3)
aliases: discharge not amounting to an acquittal

terms.gloss: A power that may be exercised one way or another.
terms.intermediate: Where the law lets the decision-maker choose rather than telling them what to do. Bail for a non-bailable offence is a discretion; bail for a bailable one is not.
terms.advanced: A discretion is never unfettered: it must be exercised for the purpose it was given, on relevant considerations, and by the body it was given to. Those three limits are where most judicial review arguments actually live.

terms.gloss: Acting with intention to cause wrongful gain or wrongful loss.
terms.intermediate: The Penal Code defines it in s 24 by reference to wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another, and s 23 defines those.
terms.advanced: Because it is defined, the English case law on what ordinary people would consider dishonest is beside the point. The definitional chain — dishonestly, wrongful gain, wrongful loss — is worth stating in full in a property offence answer, because it is where an apparently obvious element actually gets proved.

terms.gloss: Showing that a binding case turned on a fact your case lacks.
terms.intermediate: An argument that the earlier decision's reasoning does not reach your facts, because a fact it depended on is absent or different. It is the main legitimate way out of an inconvenient precedent.
terms.advanced: A difference is only a distinction if the earlier reasoning depended on it — 'that case concerned a lorry and this a van' proves nothing unless something turned on the vehicle. Done properly it is a claim about what the earlier ratio was, which is why it is really an argument about materiality. It is also the only one of the four escapes available to a court bound by the decision.

terms.gloss: A payment to members out of a company's profits.
terms.intermediate: A share of the profits paid out to shareholders. It is not a right: it arrives only if the company declares one and is permitted to pay it.
terms.advanced: That conditionality is what makes a minority holding in a small private company weak. There is usually no buyer for the shares and no dividend to compel, which is precisely the position the oppression remedy exists to address.

terms.gloss: The relationship that makes carelessness actionable.
terms.intermediate: The first element of negligence: whether this defendant owed this claimant an obligation to take reasonable care. Without it, carelessness causing loss gives no claim.
terms.advanced: The working test asks about reasonable foreseeability of harm, proximity between the parties, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty. Pure economic loss and psychiatric injury are not simply harder instances of it but categories with their own restrictive rules, and identifying them as separate questions is the step that earns the marks.
terms.source: Standard common law; the Malaysian authorities on the duty of care

terms.gloss: Take your victim as you find them.
terms.intermediate: A defendant is liable for the full extent of the injury even where an unusual susceptibility made it far worse than it would have been for someone else.
terms.advanced: It is a rule about extent, not about kind: it does not make a defendant liable for a type of damage that was never foreseeable. It extends beyond physical constitution to include, in some circumstances, the claimant's impecuniosity and pre-existing psychiatric vulnerability.

terms.gloss: General words after a list of specifics are read as limited to the same class.
terms.intermediate: 'Cars, lorries, vans and other vehicles' — the general phrase takes its scope from the specific ones before it. There must be an identifiable class for the principle to work on.
terms.advanced: The canon fails where the specifics disclose no genus, and it yields where the evident purpose of the Act points the other way — it is an aid, not a rule. Its most common misuse in an answer is to invoke it without ever saying what the class is, which is the step that does the persuading.

terms.gloss: A law as passed by a legislature.
terms.intermediate: A piece of legislation. In Malaysia the word usually points at a State law, because States make Enactments while Parliament makes Acts.
terms.advanced: The distinction carries real weight in a federal question: which list in the Ninth Schedule the subject falls under decides who could pass it at all, and a law outside the legislature's list is void under Art 4(1) whatever it says.

terms.gloss: Property committed to someone for a purpose.
terms.intermediate: The element that makes s 405 apply: the accused received the property or dominion over it lawfully, on terms that constrained what he could do with it.
terms.advanced: Its opposite in a workplace context is mere custody, where the property remains in the employer's possession and the employee only handles it. The distinction decides whether taking it is theft or criminal breach of trust, and it turns on the scope of what was committed to the person rather than on physical proximity to the goods.

terms.gloss: Extension of time, under a construction contract.
terms.intermediate: More time to finish, granted under the contract's own machinery. Which events entitle the contractor to it, and what notice they must give, are set by the contract rather than by general law.
terms.advanced: The machinery matters as much as the entitlement: a claim good on its facts can fail on a notice provision. Read the clause before advising, because standard forms differ on both triggers and timing.

terms.gloss: What a court is allowed to consider in deciding facts.
terms.intermediate: The material the court may look at — what witnesses say, and documents and things produced. Not everything true is evidence, because the Act decides what may be proved.
terms.advanced: The Malaysian Act inverts the English arrangement: Part I declares the categories of relevant fact, and nothing outside them may be proved. So the question is never whether something is relevant in the ordinary sense, but which section makes it relevant.

terms.gloss: A closed list of what may be proved and how.
terms.intermediate: Act 56. Evidence may be given of facts in issue and of such other facts as the Act declares relevant — and of no others.
terms.advanced: This is a different system from the English law of admissibility, where relevance is a general concept subject to exclusionary rules. Here the question is never simply 'is this relevant?' but 'which section makes this relevant?' If you cannot name one, the evidence does not go in, and an answer that argues fairness instead of citing a section has misunderstood the statute.

terms.gloss: The burden of putting enough evidence on a point to make it live.
terms.intermediate: Section 103 places the burden of proving any particular fact on the person who wishes the court to believe it. Unlike the legal burden, it shifts as the evidence goes in.
terms.advanced: It is the burden that is discharged by raising a point, not by persuading the court of it. An accused who raises a defence not covered by s 105 bears only this burden, and the prosecution must then disprove it to the criminal standard; where s 105 applies, the accused carries a legal burden instead.

terms.gloss: An application made without notice to the other side.
terms.intermediate: Used where giving notice would defeat the purpose — typically urgent injunctions. It carries a strict duty of full and frank disclosure.
terms.advanced: The applicant must disclose everything material, including matters that help the absent party; a breach of that duty is itself a ground for discharging the order, regardless of the merits. Ex parte relief is temporary by design, returnable on a date when the other side can be heard inter partes.
terms.source: Rules of Court 2012 O 29 and O 32

terms.gloss: Expressing one thing implies the exclusion of others.
terms.intermediate: Where a provision names some cases, the argument runs that the ones it did not name were meant to be left out.
terms.advanced: The weakest of the linguistic canons and the most over-used. A drafter's silence is often just silence — a list may be illustrative, or the omission may be an oversight — so the canon carries weight only where the enumeration looks deliberate and complete. Courts frequently say so when rejecting it.

terms.gloss: A fact that must be proved for the claim or charge to succeed.
terms.intermediate: The facts from which, either by themselves or with others, a right, liability or disability asserted in the proceeding necessarily follows.
terms.advanced: Facts in issue are fixed by the pleadings in a civil case and by the charge in a criminal one, which is why an imprecise pleading or charge causes evidential problems later. Relevant facts are a wider category: they are admissible because they bear on a fact in issue, not because they are one.

terms.gloss: The supreme law of the Federation.
terms.intermediate: The document that creates the Federation, distributes legislative power, guarantees fundamental liberties and establishes the courts. Everything else in Malaysian law is subordinate to it.
terms.advanced: Its supremacy is stated in Art 4(1) and is the reason a legislative-competence argument exists at all: in a system of parliamentary sovereignty the question cannot arise. It is also amendable, generally by a two-thirds majority in each House, which is what makes the basic structure argument — whether some features are beyond even a valid amendment — worth having.

terms.gloss: The apex court of Malaysia.
terms.intermediate: The final appellate court, and the only court that may determine invalidity for want of legislative competence. Its decisions bind every court below.
terms.advanced: Access is not as of right in most civil matters: leave to appeal is required and is granted on limited statutory grounds, so a great many disputes end at the Court of Appeal. The Federal Court may depart from its own previous decisions, but does so sparingly and with reasons, which is why the sequence of authority in a moving area is worth stating rather than just the latest case.
terms.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Federal Constitution Art 128

terms.gloss: An obligation of loyalty owed by someone trusted to act for another.
terms.intermediate: Its core is that the fiduciary must not profit from the position or allow a conflict between duty and interest without informed consent.
terms.advanced: Directors are the standard example, but the category extends to partners, agents, trustees and solicitors. The duty is one of loyalty rather than care, which is why a decision can be perfectly competent and still a breach — and why the business judgement rule protects the care duty only.
terms.source: Companies Act 2016 ss 213(1) and 218; general equitable principle

terms.gloss: A false suggestion, active concealment, or a promise made with no intention of performing.
terms.intermediate: Section 17's definition, covering acts done with intent to deceive or to induce a party to enter the contract. Mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak.
terms.advanced: The explanation to s 17 is the operative part in most problems: silence is fraud where the circumstances impose a duty to speak, or where silence is in itself equivalent to speech. Alleging fraud has procedural consequences too — it must be pleaded specifically and with particulars, and it is proved in civil proceedings on the balance of probabilities.
terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 s 17; Rules of Court 2012 O 18

terms.gloss: Consent not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake.
terms.intermediate: Section 14 defines it by what removes it, and ss 15 to 23 define each of the five. A contract requires free consent under s 10.
terms.advanced: The list is closed and each entry has a statutory definition much narrower than its everyday sense — coercion under s 15 means an act forbidden by the Penal Code or unlawful detention of property, not pressure at large. Consequences differ too: coercion, fraud and misrepresentation make the agreement voidable under s 19, while bilateral mistake as to an essential fact makes it void under s 21.

terms.gloss: A contract becoming impossible or unlawful after it is made.
terms.intermediate: Section 57(2): a contract to do an act which after it is made becomes impossible, or unlawful for a reason the promisor could not prevent, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful.
terms.advanced: Malaysian law treats this as a statutory doctrine rather than the English implied-term or construction theories, and the consequence is automatic: the contract becomes void, and s 66 governs restoration. Mere hardship, increased expense or a bad bargain do not frustrate, and self-induced impossibility is not frustration at all.

terms.gloss: The spacing algorithm scheduling the cards in this app.
terms.intermediate: A model that estimates how durable each memory is and schedules the next review for the moment recall is predicted to fall to your chosen retention.
terms.advanced: It fits its estimates to the grades you give, which is why an honest Forgot is worth more than a flattering Hard: using Hard as a soft fail inflates every subsequent interval and quietly wrecks the schedule. Raising desired retention buys marginally better recall for a lot more reviews; the usual right response to poor recall is to re-atomise the cards instead.
terms.source: FSRS-6 via ts-fsrs, vendored in this app

terms.gloss: The rights in Part II of the Constitution.
terms.intermediate: Liberty of the person, equality, freedom of movement, speech, assembly and association, freedom of religion, rights in respect of education and property. They are enforceable against the State.
terms.advanced: Two structural points decide most problems. Some rights are held by citizens only — Art 10(1) speaks of citizens where Art 5 speaks of persons — so the claimant's status is a threshold question. And most rights are subject to restriction on stated grounds, so the argument is rarely whether the right exists and almost always whether the restriction falls within a permitted head.

terms.gloss: The case that set out the three grounds of judicial review.
terms.intermediate: Shorthand for the English decision that sorted judicial review into illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety. Malaysian courts use the same frame.
terms.advanced: The name is the initials of the body in the case, not a doctrine. Cite it for the classification of grounds; the Malaysian departure on how far a court may go comes from Rama Chandran, not from here.
terms.source: Standard classification of the grounds of review

terms.gloss: Chapter IV of the Penal Code, applying to every offence in it.
terms.intermediate: Sections 76 to 106: mistake of fact, judicial acts, accident, necessity, infancy, unsoundness of mind, intoxication, consent, and private defence.
terms.advanced: Section 6 makes every offence definition subject to them, though they are not repeated in the definition. The burden of bringing yourself within one lies on the accused under s 105 of the Evidence Act, on the balance of probabilities, and the court presumes their absence — that is a genuine legal burden and not merely an evidential one.
terms.source: Penal Code ss 6 and 76-106; Evidence Act 1950 s 105

terms.gloss: Depart from the literal meaning where it produces an absurdity.
terms.intermediate: A traditional escape from a literal reading that would produce a result no legislature could have intended.
terms.advanced: Largely subsumed by the purposive direction, since an absurd result is unlikely to promote the Act's purpose. It survives as a way of describing the pressure point: the argument is really about how absurd a result has to be before the court concludes the words cannot mean what they appear to say.

terms.gloss: A promise to answer for another's default.
terms.intermediate: A promise that if someone else does not pay, you will. A bank asking a director to sign personally is asking for a guarantee.
terms.advanced: A guarantee is a secondary obligation, so it depends on the principal debt existing. It is the commonest hole in the protection of separate legal personality — not the shares and not the seat on the board, but a contract signed in the person's own name.

terms.gloss: Exception 1 to s 300 — loss of self-control reducing murder.
terms.intermediate: Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, while deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation.
terms.advanced: Both adjectives do work: the provocation must be grave, judged with some regard to the accused's situation, and sudden, which is what a cooling-off period defeats. The Exception carries provisos of its own — it does not apply where the provocation was sought or voluntarily provoked, nor where it was given by something done in obedience to the law or in the lawful exercise of private defence.

terms.gloss: An order requiring a detainer to justify the detention.
terms.intermediate: The remedy for unlawful detention: the person holding the detainee must show lawful authority for doing so, or release them.
terms.advanced: It tests the legality of the detention, not its wisdom, and it is available even where a statute purports to make the detaining authority's decision final. Under detention legislation the practical scope of the inquiry has been narrowed by statute at various times, which is why the current provisions matter as much as the principle.
terms.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(2); Criminal Procedure Code Chapter XXXVI

terms.gloss: Unlimited original jurisdiction, and the first of the superior courts.
terms.intermediate: There are two of coordinate jurisdiction: the High Court in Malaya, and the High Court in Sabah and Sarawak. Neither binds the other.
terms.advanced: Coordinate means exactly that — a decision of one is persuasive in the other, and a High Court judge is not bound by another High Court judge, though departing from one is done with reasons because inconsistency at the same level is its own mischief. The High Court is also the forum for judicial review under Order 53 and for an order for sale of land held under Registry title.
aliases: High Court in Sabah and Sarawak

terms.gloss: House of Lords — the former highest court in the United Kingdom.
terms.intermediate: The UK's top court until 2009, when the UK Supreme Court replaced it. Its decisions appear in English citations as (HL).
terms.advanced: Salomon, the case that settled separate corporate personality, is a House of Lords decision from 1897 that Malaysian courts apply. Age alone is not a reason to distrust a decision; some old ones hold up better than recent ones.

terms.gloss: A registered title that cannot be set aside.
terms.intermediate: Section 340(1): the title or interest of a registered proprietor is indefeasible, subject to the exceptions in s 340(2) — fraud or misrepresentation, forgery or an insufficient or void instrument, and unlawful acquisition.
terms.advanced: Malaysian law applies deferred, not immediate, indefeasibility: a proprietor registered through a forged or void instrument takes a defeasible title, while a subsequent purchaser in good faith and for value takes a good one. Adorna Properties held the opposite and stood for nine years before Tan Ying Hong departed from it, so anything written on the topic before 2010 must be dated before it is trusted.
terms.source: National Land Code s 340; Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC); Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Boonsom Boonyanit [2001] 1 MLJ 241 (FC)

terms.gloss: A promise to make good another's loss.
terms.intermediate: An undertaking to cover someone else's loss if it happens. It stands on its own, without needing anybody else to default first.
terms.advanced: That independence is what separates it from a guarantee: an indemnity is a primary obligation, so it survives circumstances that would discharge a surety, and it is not defeated merely because the principal obligation turns out to be unenforceable.

terms.gloss: A conclusion drawn from a proved fact rather than stated directly.
terms.intermediate: Something the court works out from other facts, instead of being told outright. Nobody saw the theft, but the goods were in his room the next morning.
terms.advanced: An inference must be the reasonable conclusion from proved facts, not a guess dressed as one. Where an inference is permissive the court may draw it and is never bound to, which is the difference between s 114's illustrations and a presumption the court must make.

terms.gloss: Mixing topics in a session rather than blocking them.
terms.intermediate: Studying contract and criminal law in the same sitting rather than one after the other. It feels worse and produces better discrimination between them.
terms.advanced: Blocked practice lets you apply the same rule repeatedly without deciding which rule applies — which is the very skill an issue-spotting problem tests. Interleaving forces the choice each time, and the cost is that performance during practice drops, which learners routinely misread as the method not working.
terms.source: Make It Stick; the interleaving literature

terms.gloss: An order holding the position until trial.
terms.intermediate: The applicant must show a serious question to be tried, that damages would not be an adequate remedy, and that the balance of convenience favours the injunction. An undertaking in damages is ordinarily required.
terms.advanced: The court does not try the merits, which is why an argument that the applicant will probably win is beside the point. A mandatory injunction — requiring something to be done rather than restrained — attracts a higher threshold, and the Malaysian gloss on American Cyanamid should be cited from a Malaysian decision rather than an English one.
terms.source: Rules of Court 2012 O 29; American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396 as applied in Malaysia

terms.gloss: Settling what a provision means.
terms.intermediate: Deciding what the words of an Act actually require. You start with the words themselves, then their place in the Act, then what the Act was for.
terms.advanced: Section 17A requires a purposive approach, so a reading that promotes the underlying object is preferred to one that does not. The internal aids — long title, marginal notes, provisos, definition sections — come before external material.

terms.gloss: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion — a structure for making reasoning visible.
terms.intermediate: A way of ordering an answer so that the rule is stated before it is used and the application is separated from the recitation. It is scaffolding, not a form to be filled.
terms.advanced: Its value is that it forces the step people skip when unsure: stating the governing rule with its source before reasoning from it. Its characteristic failure is a long Rule section and a thin Application — an answer that proves recall and not reasoning, which is why rubric bands weight application most heavily.

terms.gloss: The power to decide disputes according to law, and whether the Constitution still vests it.
terms.intermediate: Before 1988 Article 121(1) vested the judicial power of the Federation in the High Courts. The amendment replaced that with jurisdiction 'conferred by or under federal law'.
terms.advanced: On one reading the courts' jurisdiction became entirely a creature of statute; on another, judicial power is inherent in a constitution that separates the branches and cannot be removed by rewriting the sentence describing it. Malaysian courts have taken both views at different times, and this is the most unsettled area in the constitutional module — do not state either position as settled without checking the most recent Federal Court authority.

terms.gloss: The court reviewing how a public decision was made, not whether it was right.
terms.intermediate: Brought under Order 53 with leave. The grounds are illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety, with proportionality argued as a fourth.
terms.advanced: Review goes to the decision-making process, which is why it is not an appeal. Malaysian law has gone further than English law in places: R Rama Chandran allows a court in an appropriate case to examine substance and to substitute its own decision rather than remitting — though later authority has been careful about the limits, and the case should be cited for what it decided rather than for the proposition that review is now an appeal.
terms.source: Rules of Court 2012 O 53; R Rama Chandran v Industrial Court of Malaysia [1997] 1 MLJ 145 (FC)

terms.gloss: The range of people and matters a court may decide.
terms.intermediate: Whether this court is allowed to hear this case at all. It has two halves: the kind of matter, and the people or the place involved. A court without jurisdiction cannot cure that by deciding the case well.
terms.advanced: Every Malaysian court below the Constitution's own heads takes its jurisdiction from statute, so the question is always which provision confers it. Keep three things apart: whether a court has jurisdiction, whether it should exercise one it has, and whether the decision it reached was right. Only the first is jurisdiction.
terms.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Subordinate Courts Act 1948

terms.gloss: Glanville Williams, Learning the Law — the method book this course leans on.
terms.intermediate: An introduction to reading statutes and cases, solving problem questions and studying law. Edited by A. T. H. Smith, 18th edition, Sweet & Maxwell.
terms.advanced: Its framing is the English legal system, so take the method and not the substantive law. How to read a section, brief a case and structure an answer transfers to Malaysia unchanged; what the law says does not.
terms.source: Glanville Williams, Learning the Law, 18th ed (Sweet & Maxwell), ed A. T. H. Smith

terms.gloss: A registered interest giving the right to occupy land for a term.
terms.intermediate: A right to occupy someone else's land for a fixed period. A registered lease is an interest in the land itself, which is more than a tenancy agreement between two people.
terms.advanced: Registration is what makes the difference: a registered lease binds a later proprietor, while an unregistered arrangement generally binds only the parties to it. The register is where you find out which one you are dealing with.

terms.gloss: The risk of losing if the fact is not proved. It does not shift.
terms.intermediate: Section 101: whoever asserts facts on which a right or liability depends must prove them. Section 102 identifies who carries it by asking who would fail if no evidence were given.
terms.advanced: Its counterpart, the evidential burden under s 103, is the burden of adducing evidence on a particular fact, and that does move as the case develops. Saying 'the burden shifted' without saying which one is the standard imprecision in this area, and it matters most in criminal cases, where the legal burden stays on the prosecution except where a statute places one on the accused.

terms.gloss: Whether the legislature had power to pass the law at all.
terms.intermediate: Parliament may legislate on the Federal and Concurrent Lists; a State Legislature on the State and Concurrent Lists. A law outside the allotted field is invalid however sensible it is.
terms.advanced: Competence is the prior question in any constitutional problem, and it is often decisive without reaching rights at all: a restriction contained in an ultra vires statute fails before Article 10 is ever considered. The Federal Court has exclusive jurisdiction under Art 128 to determine invalidity on this ground, so getting the forum right is part of the answer.
terms.source: Federal Constitution Arts 74, 4(1) and 128; Ninth Schedule

terms.gloss: An expectation founded on a clear representation or a settled practice.
terms.intermediate: Most secure in its procedural form: that a person will be consulted or heard before a change. The substantive form — that the benefit itself will be conferred — is more contested.
terms.advanced: An expectation cannot be legitimate if the representation was outside the decision-maker's power, because a public body cannot bind itself to act unlawfully. The reception of substantive legitimate expectation in Malaysia should be checked against current authority rather than asserted, and a settled practice described in a published leaflet is exactly the kind of material that founds the procedural form.
terms.source: Standard administrative law; the Malaysian authorities on legitimate expectation

terms.gloss: What an agreed-damages clause is allowed to protect.
terms.intermediate: The innocent party's genuine commercial interest in performance, beyond simply being compensated in money. The test asks whether the stipulated sum is out of all proportion to it.
terms.advanced: It comes into Malaysian law through Cubic Electronics, which drew on Cavendish v Makdessi, and it shifted the focus away from the old genuine-pre-estimate question. Timely completion of a revenue-producing asset is the standard example of such an interest; deterrence for its own sake, unmoored from any interest in performance, is not.
terms.source: Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd [2019] 2 MLJ 806 (FC)

terms.gloss: Being legally answerable for something.
terms.intermediate: Being on the hook: the law says you must pay, compensate or answer for what happened. Establishing liability is a separate question from how much is owed.
terms.advanced: Keep liability and quantum apart in an answer. A party may be liable and owe very little, or be plainly at fault and owe nothing because the damage was too remote. Merging the two is a standard way to lose marks in tort.

terms.gloss: Defamation in permanent form.
terms.intermediate: Written, printed or otherwise recorded defamation. It is actionable without proof of special damage.
terms.advanced: How internet publication is classified has made the permanent-or-transient line harder to apply than it sounds, and the current Malaysian position should be checked rather than assumed. Each republication is generally a fresh publication, which is what makes online material a continuing exposure rather than a single event.

terms.gloss: The way a deposited title document is protected as security.
terms.intermediate: Where the issue document of title is deposited with an intention to create security, the lien is protected — and becomes enforceable — by entering a lien-holder's caveat.
terms.advanced: Facts that mention a deposited title document are almost always testing this rather than a private caveat, and recognising the cue is faster than reasoning from first principles. The lien is an informal security that the Code accommodates rather than creates, which is why the caveat does more work here than it does elsewhere.
terms.source: National Land Code, the caveat provisions

terms.gloss: The period within which an action must be brought.
terms.intermediate: Generally six years for contract and tort under the Limitation Act 1953, and twelve for actions to recover land, running from when the cause of action accrued.
terms.advanced: Accrual is not the same as the wrongful act: in contract it runs from breach, in negligence generally from when damage occurs, which may be much later. Limitation is a defence that must be pleaded, and other statutes contain their own periods — public authorities and certain claims are subject to shorter ones — so the general period must be checked against the particular claim.

terms.gloss: A sum the contract fixes as payable on breach.
terms.intermediate: An agreed figure intended to save the trouble of proving loss. In Malaysia its effect is governed by s 75 rather than by the English penalty rule.
terms.advanced: The parties' own description of the sum as a genuine pre-estimate is evidence and not conclusive; a label cannot convert a disproportionate sum into a proportionate one. Under the Cubic Electronics approach the questions are whether the clause protects a legitimate interest and whether the sum is out of all proportion to it, and causation still has to be established — a claimant cannot recover for a loss the breach did not cause.

terms.gloss: Give the words their ordinary meaning.
